claims.supporting_passage: Leonhardt 2020: "Seven studies with a total of 446 participants (mean age 82.4 ± 5.3 years) were identified. Emerging evidence shows that BCM significantly improves the ability to get up unassisted from the floor, as well as mobility with reduced fall incidence in older people. Furthermore, it can potentially reduce fear of falling. Reporting on feasibility and acceptance of BCM was limited. Study quality varied widely." Burton 2018: "meta-analyses of all RCT interventions indicated no significant change in time for older people to get up off the floor independently with intervention (MD: -0.43[-1.38, 0.51])." ... "Heterogeneity between studies was high, therefore results should be viewed with some caution." Swancutt 2020: "However, future research is required to establish whether undertaking 'getting up' training is effective and cost-effective at, for example, reducing the consequences of a long lie or ambulance callouts."
claims.location: Leonhardt 2020 Abstract; Burton 2018 Abstract; Swancutt 2020 Discussion (Implications)
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults 60+; floor-rise or backward-chaining training vs control; outcomes ability or time to rise.
claims.safe_wording: The earlier research is small and mixed. One review of 7 studies (446 people) found backward chaining improved people's ability to get up unaided; another review that pooled trials did not find a clear change in the time taken to get up. No study has yet shown that practising prevents long lies.
claims.qualifications: Evidence gap, not evidence of no benefit.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Leonhardt's mention of 'reduced fall incidence' comes from few, variable-quality studies; do not repeat it as a finding.

numbers.meaning: Leonhardt 2020 review of backward chaining
Burton 2018 pooled change in time to rise; not significant

claims.claim: Getting-up techniques are rarely taught by therapists or ambulance staff.
claims.supporting_passage: Swancutt 2020: "Neither therapists nor ambulance service staff routinely teach strategies on how to get up, meaning that healthcare professionals largely have a reactive role in managing falls." Seeley 2026 (Introduction): "Floor-rise ability is an important functional skill, recognised in international guidelines [], which is rarely taught to fallers by physiotherapists or ambulance crews [] and is frequently omitted from fall prevention programmes []."
claims.location: Swancutt 2020 Abstract, Conclusion; Seeley 2026 Introduction
claims.pico_timeframe: Swancutt: 28 older people, spouses and staff in Devon; qualitative.
claims.safe_wording: It is often not taught. In a study in Devon, neither therapists nor ambulance staff routinely showed people how to get up after a fall. That is why it is worth asking.
claims.qualifications: Qualitative, one region; Seeley's statement is background citing other work.

claims.claim: FaME (Falls Management Exercise) classes include practice at getting up from the floor.
claims.supporting_passage: "The Falls Management Exercise (FaME) programme is the only evidence-based exercise intervention for high-risk fallers that includes floor-rise training (FRT) [,] but usually only after 12 weeks of the 24-week programme."
claims.location: Seeley 2026 Introduction
claims.pico_timeframe: Background statement about a UK programme.
claims.safe_wording: Some falls prevention classes, such as FaME (Falls Management Exercise), include practice at getting up from the floor, usually from about halfway through the 24-week programme.
claims.qualifications: Background statement in a paper co-authored by FaME's developer (Skelton); the FaME trial (Skelton 2005, PMID 16267192) has no abstract in PubMed and was not opened. Do not quote the '31% fewer falls' figure from this background sentence.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Seeley calls FaME 'the only' such programme; the WFG says 'some' programmes include it. Use 'some'.

numbers.meaning: length of FaME programme; floor practice usually after week 12

claims.claim: NHS Inform in Scotland has a film ('Upwards and Onwards') on getting up after a fall.
claims.supporting_passage: Seeley 2026: "Controls viewed the NHS Inform video 'Upwards and Onwards' [], divided into segments over five 20-minute sessions including facilitated discussion." Swancutt 2020: "resources for older people and their families to enable them to practice getting up, such as the film produced by NHS Inform in Scotland [], could be a valuable supplement to face-to-face training or as a self-management resource." Seeley 2026 Discussion: "However, this did not translate to increased functional success (binary ability to rise), suggesting that while videos improve awareness, supervised practice is necessary for skill acquisition."
claims.location: Seeley 2026 Methods and Discussion; Swancutt 2020 Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Public resource named in two papers.
claims.safe_wording: NHS Inform in Scotland has a film called 'Upwards and Onwards' about getting up after a fall. In the 2026 trial, watching it without practising did not change whether people could get up, so use it alongside practice with a physiotherapist or trained instructor.
claims.qualifications: The NHS Inform page itself could not be opened; Alasdair must check the current link before it goes in source_reply.

claims.claim: People who are hurt or in pain after a fall should not try to get up and should call for help (safety line the judge requires).
claims.supporting_passage: No supporting passage found in any opened source.
claims.location: Not found
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Not verified. Until a source is opened, frame it as a question for the reader to ask: 'Ask the physiotherapist how to tell when to try to get up and when to stay put and call for help.'
claims.qualifications: The instruction is standard advice but no opened guideline or paper states it; NHS and CSP pages could not be opened.

claims.claim: A step-by-step sequence for getting up (roll onto your side, hands and knees, crawl to a sturdy chair, stronger leg forward, push up, turn and sit) copied from a verified physiotherapy guide, for the carousel.
claims.supporting_passage: No step-by-step guide was opened. Nearest verified description, Seeley 2026: "Participants were instructed to rise from half-kneeling (one knee down), side-sitting (weight on one hip) and supine (lying flat on the back) positions using a sturdy chair for support".
claims.location: Seeley 2026 Methods (Outcome measures)
claims.pico_timeframe: Assessment positions in the trial, not a public instruction sheet.
claims.safe_wording: Do not publish a step-by-step carousel from unverified steps. A visual may show the three positions practised in the trial (half-kneeling, side-sitting on one hip, lying on the back, each with a sturdy chair for support), labelled as positions practised in a 2026 trial, with 'Practise this with a physiotherapist first'.
claims.qualifications: A verified guide (for example the NHS Inform film or a CSP leaflet) must be opened before any step list is drawn.

claims.claim: Exercise programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises reduce falls; programmes that are mainly strength training, dance or walking have uncertain effects.
claims.supporting_passage: "Compared with control, balance and functional exercises reduce the rate of falls by 24% (RaR 0.76, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.81; 7920 participants, 39 studies; high-certainty evidence) and the number of people experiencing one or more falls by 13% (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.91; 8288 participants, 37 studies; high-certainty evidence). Multiple types of exercise (most commonly balance and functional exercises plus resistance exercises) probably reduce the rate of falls by 34% (RaR 0.66, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.88; 1374 participants, 11 studies; moderate-certainty evidence)" ... "Tai Chi may reduce the rate of falls by 19% (RaR 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.99; 2655 participants, 7 studies; low-certainty evidence)" ... "We are uncertain of the effects of programmes that are primarily resistance training, or dance or walking programmes on the rate of falls and the number of people who experience falls."
claims.location: Abstract, Main results (Different exercise types versus control)
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling people aged 60+; exercise type vs control; rate of falls and fallers.
claims.safe_wording: In the 2019 Cochrane review, programmes built mainly on balance and functional exercises, such as standing up from a chair and stepping, cut falls by about a quarter. Programmes that mix several types, usually balance plus strength, probably cut falls too, and Tai Chi may. For programmes that are mainly strength training, dancing or walking, the effect on falls is uncertain.
claims.qualifications: 'Uncertain' is an evidence gap, not proof of no effect. Examples of functional exercise come from the World Falls Guidelines ('e.g. sit-to-stand, stepping').

numbers.meaning: reduction in rate of falls with balance and functional exercise; 39 studies; high certainty
reduction in people with 1 or more falls, balance and functional exercise
multiple exercise types; moderate certainty
Tai Chi; low certainty

claims.claim: The balance exercises that prevented falls best were challenging exercises done standing.
claims.supporting_passage: "The greatest relative effects of exercise on fall rates (RR=0.58, 95% CI=0.48-0.69, 68% of between-study variability explained) were seen in programs that included a combination of a higher total dose of exercise (>50 hours over the trial period) and challenging balance exercises (exercises conducted while standing in which people aimed to stand with their feet closer together or on one leg, minimize use of their hands to assist, and practice controlled movements of the center of mass) and did not include a walking program."
claims.location: Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: 44 trials, 9,603 older people in the community and residential care; meta-regression.
claims.safe_wording: In the trials, the balance exercises that challenged people most were done standing: feet closer together or on one leg, using the hands less for support, and practising controlled shifts of body weight.
claims.qualifications: The 'larger effects' part is a between-trial comparison (meta-regression). The definition is what the post needs.

numbers.meaning: total exercise over the trial period in the most effective programmes (2008 meta-regression)

claims.claim: Programmes that challenged balance and involved more than about 3 hours a week had larger effects (between-trial comparison).
claims.supporting_passage: Sherrington 2017: "Overall, exercise reduced the rate of falls in community-dwelling older people by 21% (pooled rate ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.85, p<0.001, I47%, 69 comparisons) with greater effects seen from exercise programmes that challenged balance and involved more than 3 hours/week of exercise. These variables explained 76% of the between-trial heterogeneity and in combination led to a 39% reduction in falls (incident rate ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.72, p<0.001)." Sherrington 2020: "Interventions with a total weekly dose of 3+ h that included balance and functional exercises were particularly effective with a 42% reduction in rate of falls compared to control (Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR) 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.76)."
claims.location: Sherrington 2017 Abstract; Sherrington 2020 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling older people; between-trial meta-regression and subgroup analysis by weekly dose and balance challenge.
claims.safe_wording: Across trials, programmes that challenged balance and added up to 3 hours or more a week had the biggest effects. This comes from comparing different trials, not from a trial that tested different amounts, so treat 3 hours as a guide rather than a rule.
claims.qualifications: Meta-regression across trials, not a dose trial (judge's concern). Participants in higher-dose trials may differ in other ways.

numbers.meaning: weekly exercise dose linked with larger effects
Sherrington 2017: reduction in falls rate for balance-challenging, >3 h/week programmes
Sherrington 2020: reduction for 3+ h/week programmes including balance and functional exercise

claims.claim: The World Falls Guidelines recommend balance-challenging and functional exercise, three or more times a week, individualised and progressed for at least 12 weeks and continued longer; benefits are lost when people stop.
claims.supporting_passage: "We recommend exercise programmes for fall prevention for community-dwelling older adults which include balance challenging and functional exercises (e.g. sit-to-stand, stepping), with sessions three times or more weekly which are individualised, progressed in intensity for at least 12 weeks and continued longer for greater effect." (1A) "We recommend inclusion, when feasible, of Tai Chi and/or additional individualised progressive resistance strength training." (1B) "Exercise needs to be progressive initially and maintained once a plateau is reached." "Benefits of exercise are lost on cessation so opportunities to continue with appropriate activity at the end of the programme are important."
claims.location: Full text, WG4 Exercise interventions table; Component interventions, Exercise and physical activity interventions
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling older adults; guideline recommendation with GRADE 1A.
claims.safe_wording: The 2022 World Falls Guidelines recommend exercise that challenges balance and practises everyday movements such as standing up from a chair and stepping, three or more times a week, tailored to the person and made harder over time, for at least 12 weeks and kept up for longer. Strength training or Tai Chi can be added where possible. The benefits are lost when people stop.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's wording 'with resistance training' should read 'with strength training added where feasible' (separate 1B recommendation).

numbers.meaning: guideline frequency
minimum programme length, continued longer for greater effect
strength of recommendation

claims.claim: WHO 2020 guidelines advise older adults to do varied multicomponent activity emphasising balance and strength on 3 or more days a week to prevent falls (replaces the UK CMO claim, which could not be opened).
claims.supporting_passage: "As such it is recommended that as part of their weekly physical activity, older adults should do varied multicomponent physical activity at moderate or greater intensity on 3 or more days a week in order to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls." ... "Third, with respect to older adults, the recommendation regarding multicomponent physical activity that emphasises functional balance and strength training to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls now applies to all older adults rather than specifically those with poor mobility."
claims.location: Full text, Older adults section; Discussion (differences from 2010 guidelines)
claims.pico_timeframe: Global guideline for adults aged 65+.
claims.safe_wording: The World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines advise all older adults to do varied activity that focuses on balance and strength, at moderate effort or more, on 3 or more days a week, to keep up everyday abilities and prevent falls.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's UK Chief Medical Officers' claim (strength and balance on at least two days a week) was not verified: the CMO document was not in Drive and gov.uk could not be opened. Use WHO 2020 instead, or drop the CMO line.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The UK CMO figure (2 days) and WHO figure (3 days) differ; do not mix them.

numbers.meaning: WHO 2020 frequency for multicomponent balance and strength activity in older adults

claims.claim: Seated (chair-based) exercise has other benefits but has not been tested well as a way to prevent falls, and did not clearly improve balance.
claims.supporting_passage: Klempel 2021 (Abstract): "In this systematic review including 1388 participants, results demonstrated that chair-based exercise programmes improve upper extremity (handgrip strength: MD = 2.10; 95% CI = 0.76, 3.43 and 30 s arm curl test: MD = 2.82; 95% CI = 1.34, 4.31) and lower extremity function (30 s chair stand: MD 2.25; 95% CI = 0.64, 3.86)." Results: "No significant differences between groups were observed in the Berg balance scale, timed up and go test or gait speed between the intervention and control groups." Discussion: "The findings of a lack of effect on balance are in keeping with a previous review of chair-based exercise []." Anthony 2013: "The quality of the evidence base for CBEs is low with inconclusive findings to clearly inform practice."
claims.location: Klempel 2021 Abstract, Results 3.5, Discussion; Anthony 2013 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults aged 50+ (Klempel) and frail people 65+ (Anthony) in chair-based programmes; outcomes physical function; falls not an outcome.
claims.safe_wording: Seated exercise has real benefits: a 2021 review of 25 studies found chair-based classes improved arm and leg strength. But in those studies it did not clearly improve balance or walking, and none measured falls. A seated class can be a good start if you can't yet stand for long; on its own it has not been tested as a way to prevent falls.
claims.qualifications: The candidate's wording 'Seated exercise has not been shown to reduce falls (Sherrington reviews)' does not match any Sherrington review. Supportable form: an evidence gap from chair-based exercise reviews plus the standing definition of challenging balance exercise (C01-25-b). Meets the judge's values concern.

numbers.meaning: Klempel 2021 review of chair-based exercise
more chair stands in 30 seconds with chair-based exercise; practitioner use

claims.claim: For people who are frail or at higher risk, guidelines recommend more supervision or smaller groups, and exercise adapted to their abilities.
claims.supporting_passage: "Exercise programmes that need to be of sufficient intensity and duration should be delivered in a way that ensures safety and considers functional abilities." ... "Higher supervision levels or smaller group numbers are recommended for those at higher risk of a fall including those who are frail [,]."
claims.location: Full text, Exercise and physical activity interventions (Recommendation details and justification)
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults at higher falls risk, including frail people.
claims.safe_wording: If you are frail or have fallen before, the guidelines recommend classes with more supervision or smaller groups, run in a way that keeps you safe and suits what you can do.
claims.qualifications: None.

claims.claim: If no suitable class exists, exercise can be taught as an individual home programme; the Otago home programme reduced falls.
claims.supporting_passage: WFG: "Exercise programmes can be delivered in a group or taught and supported as an individualised home exercise programme or a mix of both in order to achieve an effective dose [,]." Thomas 2010: "seven trials, involving 1503 participants were included. The mean age of participants was 81.6 (±3.9) years." ... "and significantly reduced fall rates (incidence rate ratio = 0.68, 95% CI = 0.56-0.79)." ... "Of the 747 participants who remained in the studies at 12 months, 274 (36.7%) were still exercising three or more times per week."
claims.location: WFG full text, Exercise section; Thomas 2010 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Community-dwelling adults aged 65+ (mean 81.6); Otago home strength and balance programme vs control; falls rate over about 12 months.
claims.safe_wording: If there is no suitable class near you, ask about a home programme. The guidelines say exercise can be taught as an individual home programme, or a mix of home and group sessions. A review of 7 trials of the Otago home programme (1503 people, average age 82) found it cut the rate of falls by about a third.
claims.qualifications: 2010 review; do not use its mortality finding. Adherence fell over time (about 37 in 100 still exercising 3 times a week at 12 months).

numbers.meaning: Otago: rate ratio for falls, about 32% fewer falls
Otago review
still exercising 3 or more times a week at 12 months

claims.claim: Hospital falls are commonly reported as falls per 1000 occupied bed days.
claims.supporting_passage: NAIF 2015: "Falls per 1,000 OBDs We report, for the first time, current falls rates across most hospitals in England and Wales. The average number of falls per 1,000 OBDs is 6.63" and "Clinical staff and hospital managers should review the total number of falls and the number of falls with an outcome of harm per 1,000 OBDs." Healey 2008: "Falls rates were standardised as number of falls per 1,000 occupied bed days." Pu 2025: "[95 %, one-tailed, non-inferiority confidence limit of 2.00 falls/1000 occupied bed days (OBDs) increase]"
claims.location: NAIF 2015 Key findings and Recommendations; Healey 2008 Abstract; Pu 2025 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Acute hospitals in England and Wales (2014 data); NRLS 2005 to 2006; Australian wards 2023 to 2024.
claims.safe_wording: Hospitals usually count falls as falls per 1000 occupied bed days. The Royal College of Physicians' national audit used this measure (2015 report, average 6.63 falls per 1000 bed days in England and Wales), and trials still use it.
claims.qualifications: The NAIF report opened is from 2015; current NAIF metrics were not verified. Use present tense only for 'commonly used', not for current national figures.

numbers.meaning: mean falls per 1000 occupied bed days, England and Wales hospitals, 2014 data (NAIF 2015)
range across organisations (NAIF 2015); reflects reporting differences too

claims.claim: The national audit itself warned that a low falls rate does not necessarily mean good care.
claims.supporting_passage: "A low number of falls per 1,000 OBDs does not necessarily mean the trust or LHB performed well in the clinical audit." ... "Therefore comparisons need to be made with caution, as hospitals with higher than average reported rates of falls may have better reporting, or better falls prevention care for more vulnerable patients. Conversely, organisations with very low rates may have a poor culture of defining or reporting falls rather than having robust approaches for prevention of falls."
claims.location: NAIF 2015, Falls reporting (Falls per 1,000 OBDs caveats)
claims.pico_timeframe: NHS hospital trusts and health boards, England and Wales.
claims.safe_wording: The national audit itself warned that a low falls rate does not necessarily mean a hospital is doing well, because a very low rate can reflect poor reporting.
claims.qualifications: The audit's stated reason is under-reporting, not immobility. Do not imply the audit said wards keep patients in bed.

claims.claim: Older people in hospital spend most of their time lying in bed, including many who can walk.
claims.supporting_passage: Brown 2009: "Forty-five male patients (mean age 74.2) with a mean length of stay of 5.1 days generated 2,592 one-hour periods of data. A baseline functional assessment indicated that 35 (77.8%) study patients were willing and able to walk a short distance independently. No patient remained in bed the entire measured hospital stay, but on average, 83% of the measured hospital stay was spent lying in bed. The average amount of time that any one individual spent standing or walking ranged from a low of 0.2% to a high of 21%, with a median of 3%, or 43 minutes per day." Pedersen 2013: "The ambulatory patients were lying median 17 hours, (interquartile range [IQR]: 14.4-19.1), sitting 5.1 hours (IQR: 2.9-7.1), and standing and/or walking 1.1 hours (IQR: 0.6-1.7) per day."
claims.location: Brown 2009 Abstract, Results; Pedersen 2013 Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Brown: 45 male medical inpatients 65+, one US VA hospital, first 7 days, accelerometers. Pedersen: 43 ambulatory older medical patients, Copenhagen, accelerometers throughout stay.
claims.safe_wording: Older people in hospital spend most of the day in bed, including many who can walk. In a US veterans' hospital, 45 men aged 65 and over spent on average 83% of their measured time lying in bed, and the typical time standing or walking was 43 minutes a day. In a Danish study of 43 older medical patients who could walk, the typical time lying down was 17 hours a day.
claims.qualifications: Small cohorts, one US hospital (men only, 2009) and one Danish hospital (2013). Give Brown 2009 as one US hospital cohort (judge's concern). Do not use Growdon's '95% of their time in bed' figure (background estimate).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Other small accelerometer studies found by Consensus (not opened) report lying for about 50 to 60% of recorded time in some settings; figures vary by setting and method.

numbers.meaning: average proportion of measured hospital stay spent lying in bed, 45 men 65+, first 7 days
time standing or walking, Brown 2009
time lying, 43 ambulatory older medical patients, Pedersen 2013
Brown 2009 patients able to walk a short distance independently at baseline

claims.claim: Low mobility in hospital is associated with loss of function, new institutionalisation and death, and much bed rest has no documented medical reason.
claims.supporting_passage: "When compared with the high mobility group, the low and intermediate groups were associated with the adverse outcomes in a graded fashion, even after controlling for multiple confounders." ... "Bedrest was ordered at some point during hospitalization in 165 (33%) patients. For most patients, mobility was limited involuntarily (bedrest orders), and almost 60% of bedrest episodes in the lowest mobility group had no documented medical indication."
claims.location: Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: 498 medical inpatients aged 70+, US university teaching hospital; exposure average mobility level; outcomes ADL decline, new institutionalisation, death; adjusted odds ratios.
claims.safe_wording: Low mobility in hospital is linked with worse outcomes. In a US study of 498 medical patients aged 70 and over, those who moved least were more likely to lose everyday abilities, move into a care home or die, even after allowing for how ill they were. That link does not prove the lack of movement caused the harm. A third had bed rest ordered, and almost 60% of bed rest episodes in the least mobile group had no recorded medical reason.
claims.qualifications: Observational; sicker patients move less (reverse causation possible). Do not convert the adjusted odds ratios. Covinsky 2011 (PMID 22028354) is a review that puts hospital-associated disability at about one third of patients over 70; not needed.

numbers.meaning: patients aged 70+
patients with bed rest ordered at some point
bed rest episodes in the lowest mobility group without documented medical indication

claims.claim: Pressure to prevent falls has been linked with restricting patients' movement.
claims.supporting_passage: King 2018: "Intense messaging from hospital administration to achieve zero falls resulted in nurses developing a fear of falls, protecting self and unit, and restricting fall risk patients as a way to stop messages and meet the hospital goal." Capo-Lugo 2023: "Non-ambulatory status, the primary outcome, was defined as a median Johns Hopkins Highest Level of Mobility <6 (i.e., patient walks less than 10 steps) throughout hospitalization." ... "8% of patients at low risk for falls were non-ambulatory, compared to 25% and 54% of patients at moderate and high risk for falls, respectively." ... "Patients categorized into higher fall risk groups had decreased mobility throughout their hospitalization, even when they had the functional capacity to ambulate." Growdon 2017: "Our current system of “keeping score” of falls has created a strong disincentive for mobilizing patients."
claims.location: King 2018 Abstract (Results); Capo-Lugo 2023 Abstract; Growdon 2017 full text
claims.pico_timeframe: King: 27 US nurses and nursing assistants, qualitative. Capo-Lugo: 48,271 adult inpatients, one US hospital, retrospective, adjusted for capacity to walk and other factors. Growdon: expert viewpoint, US.
claims.safe_wording: There is evidence that pressure to prevent falls can restrict movement. In interviews with 27 US hospital nurses and nursing assistants, 'zero falls' messages from managers led staff to restrict patients at risk of falling. In a US hospital study of 48,271 adult patients, 54% of those labelled high falls risk were recorded as mostly not walking (fewer than 10 steps), against 8% of those labelled low risk, and the gap remained among patients who were able to walk.
claims.qualifications: US evidence under a 'never event' payment context; UK practice may differ. Capo-Lugo is observational and includes adults of all ages. Keep criticism on the metric and the incentive, not on nurses (judge's values concern).

numbers.meaning: nurses and nursing assistants interviewed (King 2018)
adult inpatients (Capo-Lugo 2023)
non-ambulatory patients among those labelled low, moderate and high falls risk

claims.claim: Patients who stay at bed level fall less than those starting to move, but patients who walk fall least of all.
claims.supporting_passage: "Interestingly, the relationship between mobility performance using JH‐HLM and fall incidence followed an inverse U‐shaped curve (Figure, Panel C). Patients with JH‐HLM scores of 1 or 2, which indicate limited mobility performance at bed level, experienced fewer falls compared to those with moderate mobility performance, who move in the transition zone between bed level and walking. Conversely, patients with high mobility performance, as reflected by JH‐HLM scores of 6 or higher—which represent increasing walking distances—had the lowest incidence of falls." Discussion: "Patients who stay in bed and perform extremely low levels of activity (e.g., bed‐level activity) have lower fall incidence, but importantly, their fall rates are still higher than those of patients who were ambulatory early in their hospitalisation."
claims.location: Results; Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: 54,206 adult inpatients (498 fallers), three Maryland hospitals, 2022 to 2023; mobility performance recorded in first 48 h; unadjusted LOESS curves.
claims.safe_wording: In a study of 54,206 adult patients in three US hospitals, patients who stayed at bed level had fewer falls than patients who were starting to move between bed and walking. Patients who were walking had the fewest falls of all.
claims.qualifications: Exploratory, unadjusted, all adult ages (mean about 61). This supports the logic that a ward could see fewer falls if fewer people start to move, but it does not show that any ward lowered its rate this way.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Walking patients had the lowest falls, so promoting mobility is not the same as raising falls.

numbers.meaning: adult inpatients analysed

claims.claim: Wards lower their falls rates by keeping people in bed (direct evidence).
claims.supporting_passage: No opened source shows a ward or hospital lowering its falls rate by immobilising patients.
claims.location: Not found
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Present this as a limitation of the measure, marked as judgement: 'A falls rate on its own can't show whether falls went down because care improved or because people moved less.'
claims.qualifications: Judge's accuracy concern confirmed. The opening line 'A ward can lower its falls rate by keeping people in bed, and the falls figure will record that as an improvement' should be reworded as a statement about what the measure can and can't show.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Hoyer 2025 (C01-05-f) and King 2018 (C01-05-e) make the concern plausible; they do not measure it.

claims.claim: A mobility measure already exists and is recorded routinely in some hospitals; a project that raised mobility did not increase injurious falls.
claims.supporting_passage: Hoyer 2025 (Methods): "The JH‐HLM is an 8‐point scale documented based on the patient's observedmobility (ranging from 1 = lying in bed to 8 = walking 250+ feet). It is also required to be recorded at least once per shift by nursing staff and after every therapy session." Hoyer 2016: "Comparing the ramp-up versus post-QI phases, patients reaching JH-HLM's ambulation status increased from 43% to 70% (P < 0.001)" ... "Increased mobility was not associated with an increase in injurious falls compared to 12 months prior on the QI units (P = 0.73)."
claims.location: Hoyer 2025 Methods; Hoyer 2016 Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: Johns Hopkins health system hospitals, Maryland; Hoyer 2016: 3,352 patients on 2 general medicine units, before-after QI, 2013 to 2014.
claims.safe_wording: Some hospitals already record mobility next to falls. In Johns Hopkins hospitals in the US, nurses record each patient's highest level of mobility at least once a shift on an 8-point scale, from lying in bed to walking 250 feet or more. A quality improvement project there raised the share of patients who walked from 43% to 70%, with no rise in falls causing injury.
claims.qualifications: Before-after design, not a trial; injurious falls only; US general medicine, adults of all ages. Meets the judge's request for a named service that already reports a mobility measure; no UK example was found in opened sources.

numbers.meaning: Johns Hopkins Highest Level of Mobility, 1 = lying in bed to 8 = walking 250+ feet
recording frequency
patients reaching walking status, before vs after the QI project
no significant change in injurious falls

claims.claim: Experts have proposed that hospitals measure mobility (for example times out of bed or walks per shift) alongside falls, and adjust falls metrics for the benefits of mobility.
claims.supporting_passage: "The CMS should develop quality measures that promote mobility as part of routine clinical care, such as early mobilization protocols for hospital staff, mobility aides, and trained volunteers. Associated process measures might focus on documentation of number of times patients are out of bed or episodes of ambulation per nursing shift." ... "As more data regarding mobility are systematically collected, it will be important to ensure that current fall prevention metrics are adjusted to reflect the counterbalancing benefits of increased mobility."

claims.claim: Measures that restrict movement, such as bed alarms and restraints, lack good evidence for preventing hospital falls.
claims.supporting_passage: Shorr 2012: "An intervention designed to increase bed alarm use in an urban hospital increased alarm use but had no statistically or clinically significant effect on fall-related events or physical restraint use." WFG: "There is currently no robust research evidence to recommend the use of (i) bed/chair alarms, (ii) grip socks/non-slip socks for the purpose of falls prevention and (iii) the use of physical restraints when the sole purpose is falls prevention in hospitals."
claims.location: Shorr 2012 Abstract, Conclusion; WFG full text, Falls in hospitals
claims.pico_timeframe: Shorr: 27,672 inpatients, 16 units, one US hospital, 18 months. WFG: hospital recommendations.
claims.safe_wording: Measures that limit movement have weak evidence for preventing falls: a US trial that increased bed alarm use did not reduce falls, and the World Falls Guidelines found no strong research evidence for bed or chair alarms or physical restraints to prevent falls in hospital.
claims.qualifications: Earlier posts (E166) covered alarms; use this only as supporting context, not as the argument.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Pu 2025 found reducing mobilisation alarm use was not inferior to usual care; complete elimination was uncertain.

candidates.reason: All essential claims verified in the VISIBLE full text and the World Falls Guidelines: lower-lens blur (mechanism), overall null result (IRR 0.92, 0.73 to 1.16), pre-planned subgroup benefit in people often outdoors (IRR 0.60) and more outdoor falls in people rarely outdoors (IRR 1.56), plus adherence (54%) and more non-fall injuries (26% vs 17%). The post must lead with the overall result, call the subgroups pre-planned, include the harm and the non-fall injuries, and avoid converting Lord 2002's odds ratio. A published erratum to VISIBLE exists but could not be opened; figures used match abstract and Table 2. Allocate to C01 or C14, not both.

Cochrane 2019 figures verified from the abstract (rate ratio 0.77; risk ratio 0.85; 195 fewer falls and 72 fewer fallers per 1000 people followed for a year). Wording fixes: the denominator is '1000 people followed over one year', not 'per 1000 person-years'; say what each number counts rather than claiming a minority has most falls; state that the fallers figure is an average, not an individual prediction. The ProFaNE consensus claim (Lamb 2005) could not be verified and should be dropped; Cochrane methods (both outcomes as critical outcomes) support the position instead. The 2026 Cochrane multifactorial review (falls rate may fall by about a quarter, fallers little or no change; low certainty) gives a sharper example and supports the opening line.

Core facts verified (Tinetti 47% of non-injured fallers; Fleming 80% of fallers over 90 could not get up, 30% lay an hour or more; WFG treats an hour or more on the floor as high risk and recommends relearning by backward chaining; 2026 pilot RCT showed practice improves ability). But: Tinetti did not show significant links with hospital admission or long-term care (only lasting ADL decline 35% vs 26%); Fleming's care-home link weakened after adjustment; no study shows practice prevents long lies; the step-by-step carousel could not be verified from any opened guide; the judge's required 'don't try if hurt' safety line has no opened source.
candidates.revised_angle: Keep the 'Ask this' question ('Has anyone asked whether you can get up off the floor on your own?'). Facts: many older people who fall can't get up unaided (about half of non-injured fallers aged 72+ in a 1993 US study; 4 in 5 fallers over 90 in Cambridge), long lies are linked with harm, and the World Falls Guidelines count an hour or more on the floor as high risk and say the skill is best relearnt by practice. Action: ask a physiotherapist or falls class (for example FaME) to check whether you can get up and to help you practise; a 2026 Scottish pilot found five short sessions got everyone in the practice group able to get up from lying on their back. Say practice builds skill and confidence; do not claim it prevents long lies. Replace the step-by-step carousel with the three trial positions labelled as such, or a question card, unless a verified guide is opened. Phrase safety as a question to ask ('when should I stay put and call for help?') until a source is found. Pair with C01-21 as the judge suggested.

candidates.reason: All four questions are supported: standing balance challenge (Sherrington 2008 definition; Cochrane 2019 type analysis), progression and frequency (WFG: 3+ sessions a week, progressed, at least 12 weeks and continued; WHO 2020: 3+ days a week), and dose (3+ hours a week, a between-trial finding to present as a guide). Wording fixes: replace the UK CMO claim (not opened) with WHO 2020; describe seated exercise as having other benefits (arm and leg strength) but not tested for falls and without clear balance gains, not as 'shown not to work'; soften the opening from 'spend most of it standing up' to 'include balance exercises done standing up'. Home programme option (WFG; Otago IRR 0.68) covers the judge's sharpen, and WFG supervision advice covers frailer readers.

Supporting facts verified: falls per 1000 occupied bed days is the standard metric (NAIF 2015, Healey 2008, Pu 2025); the audit itself warned a low rate does not mean good care; older inpatients spend most time in bed (Brown 2009, Pedersen 2013); low mobility is linked with poor outcomes (Brown 2004); zero-falls pressure led US nurses to restrict patients (King 2018) and high-risk labels are linked with not walking (Capo-Lugo 2023); bed-level patients fall less than those starting to move but walkers fall least (Hoyer 2025); Johns Hopkins records a mobility score every shift and raised walking without more injurious falls (Hoyer 2016). No opened source shows a ward actually lowering its falls rate by immobilising people, and walking patients fell least, so the angle 'the easiest way to lower a falls rate is less movement' overstates the evidence.
candidates.revised_angle: Frame as a limitation of the measure (What gets counted). A falls rate on its own can't tell good falls prevention from people moving less (judgement). Evidence: older people already spend most of a hospital day in bed; in US hospitals, pressure for 'zero falls' led staff to restrict patients, and patients labelled high risk walked less even when able; patients kept at bed level fell less than those starting to move, though walkers fell least; the national audit itself said a low rate isn't proof of good care. Named measure: record each patient's highest level of mobility each shift, as Johns Hopkins hospitals do (8-point scale from lying in bed to walking 250 feet), where raising walking from 43% to 70% of patients brought no rise in injurious falls. Position (judgement): report falls per 1000 bed days next to a mobility measure. Keep criticism on the metric, not on nurses or managers. Visual stays labelled 'Illustrative, no real data'.
